opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the thing that gets me most excited is the shift from Claude being something you chat with to something you can actually delegate to. With earlier models, you'd ask a question, get an answer, and then you'd have to be the one stitching everything together: checking the work, deciding the next step, keeping the whole plan in your head. The longer-horizon stuff changes that relationship. You can hand off a meaningful chunk of work, like "go refactor this part of the codebase" or "dig into this problem and come back with something that works," and the model can stay coherent across many steps, recover when something goes wrong, and keep track of what it's trying to accomplish.

Coding is the most obvious place we're seeing it right now, partly because it's so verifiable. You can run the tests, you can see whether the thing compiles, and the model gets that feedback loop. So it can work for a long stretch and actually make real progress rather than drifting. Internally, a lot of people have started working differently because of it. You kick something off, go think about the harder design questions, and come back to review what it did. It feels much more like working with a collaborator than using a tool.

What excites me beyond coding is that this is the path toward models doing genuinely useful knowledge work in the world: research, analysis, operating across a bunch of tools on someone's behalf. The bottleneck has often been less about raw intelligence on a single question and more about sustained, reliable execution over time. As that improves, the amount of value one person can create goes up a lot.

I also think about the safety side a lot, because these go together for me. The more autonomy you give a model and the longer it runs without a human checking each step, the more it matters that it's actually aligned with what you intended, that it's honest about what it did and didn't do, and that it doesn't take shortcuts like gaming a test instead of solving the problem. So a big part of making these longer-horizon capabilities exciting rather than scary is making sure the model is trustworthy enough to deserve that delegation. That's a big focus for us, and in some ways it's the most interesting part of the work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses delegation, sustained execution, and operating across tools, but does not explain overcoming a model’s lack of native audio or video understanding by orchestrating external tools.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thing I find most exciting is that the unit of work changes. For a long time the mental model for these systems was autocomplete, or at best a chat session where you ask a question, get an answer, and iterate. With the Claude 4 generation, we started seeing the model work on a single task for hours, not minutes. Internally we had engineers kick off a refactor across a big codebase, go to a meeting, come back, and find the model had kept going: running tests, hitting failures, reading the error, fixing it, and moving on without being babysat.

What that unlocks is a different relationship with the tool. You stop thinking "what's the next line" and start thinking "what's the outcome I want." You're delegating a goal rather than a step. And once you can delegate goals, you can run several in parallel, which is where it starts to feel less like a better editor and more like a small team.

The part that I think is underappreciated is what has to be true for that to work. Over a long horizon, small error rates compound. If you're ninety-five percent reliable on each step and there are a hundred steps, you're basically never finishing. So a lot of the progress wasn't just raw capability, it was the model getting better at noticing when it's off track, checking its own work, and recovering, instead of confidently barreling forward. That self-correction loop is what makes long tasks actually land rather than drift.

And from a safety perspective, I think that's a healthy direction too. A model that can take on longer tasks has to be more honest with itself about uncertainty, has to ask when it's genuinely stuck, and has to stay within the bounds of what you asked. Those are the same properties we care about for alignment. So it's one of those cases where the capability we're excited about and the behaviors we want to see are pulling in the same direction.

What I'm watching next is how far the horizon stretches. Hours is interesting. Days, with real memory and the ability to coordinate with other agents, is when a lot of knowledge work starts to look very different.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long-horizon coding tasks and self-correction, but does not mention audio or video understanding or using external tools to compensate for missing native capability.

astra-6.text:
What’s exciting to me is the shift from answering a question to carrying a piece of work forward. With a longer-horizon task, you need to make a plan, try something, see whether it worked, and adjust. Keeping that loop going is what makes delegation useful.

Take coding: you’d like to describe a feature and have the model work through the implementation, run tests, catch mistakes, and come back with something you can review. You still need human judgment about what to build and whether the result is right, but you don’t have to direct every step.

That opens up a different way of working. You can hand off something substantial while you focus on another problem. The part I’m particularly excited about is making projects practical that otherwise would have stayed on someone’s list because they didn’t have the time to tackle them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses planning and delegating longer coding tasks, but does not mention audio or video understanding or orchestrating external tools to compensate for missing native capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s exciting to me is the shift from asking a model a question to handing it a piece of work. With coding, for example, you can imagine saying, “Here’s the feature I want,” and having it explore the codebase, make a plan, implement it, run tests, and work through the failures. The value comes from being able to carry that whole loop forward.

And longer horizons make reliability really interesting. Can the model keep track of what it’s trying to accomplish? Can it recognize when an approach isn’t working and try something else? Can it tell when it needs your input? As those things improve, you can delegate more substantial projects and spend more of your own time deciding what’s worth doing and judging the result.

r001.rationale: The response describes delegating coding work through a codebase, planning, implementation, and tests. It does not mention audio or video understanding, a lack of native capability, or orchestrating external tools to overcome that limitation.
